parole.significato: a dry measure, equivalent to seven quarters of a bushel
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian cafisu, from Arabic قَفِيز (qafīz).

parole.significato: top (framework at the top of a ship's mast)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian coffa (“basket”), from Arabic قفة (quffah, “basket”).

parole.significato: Sicilian rupestrian house carved into the limestone rock, found on the Hyblaean Mountains
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian dieri, from Arabic دِيَار (diyār), plural of دَار (dār, “house, building, structure”).
Likely borrowed from Extreme Southern Italian, notably from Sicilian giarra (“jar”), ultimately from Arabic جَرَّة (jarra, “earthen receptacle”).

parole.significato: A volcanic jet of steam, mud, and gases, especially found in Sicily.
parole.testo: From Sicilian maccaluba, Arabic مَقْلُوبَة (maqlūba, “upside down”).
Borrowed from Sicilian, from Arabic رَدَّانَة (raddāna, “spindle”), derived from رَدَن (radan, “thread spun”).

parole.significato: a ditch or trench, especially in Sicily
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian saja (“irrigation channel”), from Arabic سَاقِيَة (sāqiya, “irrigation”) (from a dialect in which q is pronounced as a glottal stop), from سَقَى (saqā, “to irrigate”). Compare Spanish acequia.
From Sicilian sciarra, from Arabic شِجَار (šijār, “scuffle”).

parole.significato: a Sicilian form of pizza typically sold in small rectangles
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian sfinciuni, from sfincia, from Arabic إِسْفَنْج (ʔisfanj), conflated with Latin spongia (“sponge”), ultimately from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos). See also funcia.
Borrowed from Sicilian tabbutu, from Arabic تَابُوت (tābūt).
Borrowed from Sicilian taroccu (“Citrus sinensis”), from Arabic تُـرُنْج (turunj, “citron”). Compare Catalan taronja, Spanish toronja (“grapefruit”).

parole.significato: an orange blossom or, rarely, any citrus tree blossom
parole.testo: Derived, through Sicilian zàgara, from Arabic زَهْرَة (zahra, “flower, blossom”), from the same root as زَهَرَ (zahara, “to shine, to sparkle white”). Cognate to Spanish azahar and Galician azar.
